question: Under RELRA Section 606, what relationship do licensees employed by a broker bear to a consumer, as compared to the broker's own relationship with that consumer?
choice_a: The same relationship the broker bears to the consumer, except that the broker may designate a licensee to act exclusively as agent of a particular seller/landlord and another licensee to act exclusively as agent of a particular buyer/tenant
choice_b: A completely independent relationship, unrelated to whatever relationship the broker itself has with the consumer
choice_c: Licensees are always treated as transaction licensees regardless of the broker's designated relationship
choice_d: Licensees may never be designated to represent one side exclusively -- only the broker itself can hold an exclusive designation
explanation: Section 606 provides that licensees employed by a broker bear the same relationship to the consumer as the broker, with the specific exception that the broker (including one serving as a dual agent) may designate a licensee to act exclusively as agent of a particular seller/landlord and another to act exclusively as agent of a particular buyer/tenant.

question: Under RELRA Section 606, in which capacities may a broker act in a real estate transaction?
choice_a: As a seller/landlord agent, a buyer/tenant agent, a dual agent for both seller/landlord and buyer/tenant, or as a transaction licensee
choice_b: Only as a seller's agent or a buyer's agent -- no other capacities are recognized
choice_c: As a fiduciary trustee only, regardless of which party engaged the broker
choice_d: As an independent contractor exclusively, with no agency capacity at all
explanation: Section 606 identifies the four capacities in which a Pennsylvania broker may act in a transaction: seller/landlord agent, buyer/tenant agent, dual agent for both, or transaction licensee -- the framework that the more detailed duty sections (606.1-606.6) then build out.

question: Among the non-waivable duties every licensee owes to ALL consumers under RELRA Section 606.1(a), what standard of skill and care applies under paragraph (1)?
choice_a: To exercise reasonable professional skill and care which meets the practice standards required by RELRA
choice_b: No specific skill/care standard is imposed by statute -- it is left entirely to each brokerage's internal policy
choice_c: A strict-liability standard under which any consumer dissatisfaction constitutes a breach
choice_d: The skill-and-care standard applies only once a written agency agreement is signed
explanation: Section 606.1(a)(1) is the first of the non-waivable general duties: exercising reasonable professional skill and care that meets RELRA's practice standards, owed to every consumer regardless of whether any agency relationship exists.

question: Which non-waivable duty is imposed by RELRA Section 606.1(a)(2), applying to a licensee regardless of any agency relationship?
choice_a: To deal honestly and in good faith
choice_b: To advocate zealously only for the party paying the licensee's fee
choice_c: To disclose the identity of every prospective buyer to the seller's attorney
choice_d: To obtain Commission pre-approval before showing any property
explanation: Section 606.1(a)(2) requires a licensee to deal honestly and in good faith with all consumers -- one of the baseline duties that applies even outside any formal agency relationship.

question: Under RELRA Section 606.1(a)(3), may the duty to present written offers to a seller in a timely manner ever be waived?
choice_a: Yes -- but only by a seller whose property is subject to an existing contract for sale, and only if the waiver is in writing and made in the manner the Commission prescribes by regulation
choice_b: No -- the duty to timely present written offers can never be waived under any circumstances
choice_c: Yes -- any buyer may waive the duty on the seller's behalf simply by submitting a low offer
choice_d: Yes -- a broker may unilaterally waive it without any involvement from the seller
explanation: Section 606.1(a)(3) requires timely presentation of written offers, notices, and communications, but carves out a narrow waiver: a seller whose property is already under an existing contract for sale may waive the duty to have further written offers presented, provided the waiver is in writing and follows the Commission's prescribed manner.

question: RELRA Section 606.1(a)(5) requires a licensee to account for consumer money and property in what manner, and consistent with which other RELRA provision?
choice_a: In a timely manner, consistent with Section 608.5's escrow and deposit-handling requirements
choice_b: Only at the annual license-renewal audit, consistent with Section 404.1
choice_c: Only upon the consumer's written demand, with no other timing requirement
choice_d: Section 606.1(a)(5) imposes no accounting duty -- that duty exists only in Commission regulations, not the statute
explanation: Section 606.1(a)(5) requires a licensee to account in a timely manner for all money and property received from or on behalf of any consumer to a transaction, consistent with the escrow-handling provisions of Section 608.5.

question: Under RELRA Section 606.1(a)(7), what must a licensee do regarding conflicts of interest?
choice_a: Timely disclose to the consumer any conflicts of interest
choice_b: Resolve every conflict of interest in the consumer's favor without disclosure
choice_c: Disclose conflicts of interest only if the consumer specifically asks
choice_d: Refer the consumer to another brokerage whenever any conflict arises
explanation: Section 606.1(a)(7) imposes a non-waivable duty to timely disclose to the consumer any conflicts of interest -- an ongoing obligation echoed again in the written-agreement disclosures required under Section 608.1(7).

question: Under RELRA Section 606.1(a)(8), what must a licensee do regarding matters beyond the licensee's own expertise?
choice_a: Advise the consumer to seek expert advice on matters relating to the transaction that are beyond the licensee's expertise
choice_b: Personally render expert advice on any subject the consumer raises, regardless of the licensee's own expertise
choice_c: Refrain from ever recommending that the consumer consult another professional
choice_d: Require the consumer to sign a liability waiver before discussing anything outside real estate brokerage
explanation: Section 606.1(a)(8) requires a licensee to advise the consumer to seek expert advice on matters relating to the transaction that fall outside the licensee's own expertise -- for example, legal, tax, or structural questions.

question: Under RELRA Section 606.1(a)(10), what must a licensee advise the consumer about regarding the transaction itself?
choice_a: The status of the transaction
choice_b: Status updates need only be provided if the consumer requests them in writing
choice_c: Status updates need only be provided to the party who is paying the commission
choice_d: No such duty exists under Section 606.1
explanation: Section 606.1(a)(10) requires the licensee to advise the consumer regarding the status of the transaction, a non-waivable duty owed to all consumers regardless of formal agency status.

question: Under RELRA Section 606.1(a)(11), what three things must a licensee do to help the consumer through settlement?
choice_a: Advise the consumer of tasks that must be completed to satisfy an agreement or condition for settlement, provide assistance with document preparation, and advise the consumer regarding compliance with laws pertaining to real estate transactions
choice_b: Personally complete all settlement conditions on the consumer's behalf without any consumer involvement
choice_c: Advise only on document preparation, with no duty to address settlement conditions or legal compliance
choice_d: This duty applies only to buyer's agents, not to seller's agents
explanation: Section 606.1(a)(11) bundles three related duties: advising on tasks needed to satisfy settlement conditions, assisting with document preparation, and advising on compliance with laws pertaining to real estate transactions.

question: Under RELRA Section 606.1(a)(12), when may a licensee decline to present an offer or counteroffer in a timely manner?
choice_a: Only if a party has directed the licensee otherwise in writing -- offers and counteroffers must otherwise be presented in a timely manner
choice_b: The licensee may present only the highest offer received, discarding all lower competing offers, without any written direction
choice_c: The licensee may decline to present any offer once a Commission investigation is pending
choice_d: A party may waive this duty verbally; no writing is ever required
explanation: Section 606.1(a)(12) requires timely presentation of all offers and counteroffers unless a party has directed the licensee otherwise in writing -- the writing requirement parallels the written-waiver mechanism in Section 606.1(a)(3).

question: Under RELRA Section 606.1(a)(13), what financial-interest disclosure must a licensee make to a consumer?
choice_a: Any financial interest, including a referral fee or commission, that the licensee or an affiliated licensee has in other services provided to the consumer by any other person, such as financial services, title, insurance, construction, repair, or inspection services
choice_b: Only financial interests exceeding $1,000 in value
choice_c: Only financial interests in title insurance companies, which are exempt from any other referral-relationship disclosure
choice_d: Financial-interest disclosure is required only in commercial transactions
explanation: Section 606.1(a)(13) requires disclosure of any financial interest a licensee (or an affiliated licensee) has in third-party services the consumer may purchase -- financial services, title, insurance, construction, repair, or inspection services, among others.

question: Under RELRA Section 606.1(a)(13), WHEN must a licensee make the required financial-interest disclosure about a referral service?
choice_a: At the time the licensee first recommends the consumer purchase the service in which the licensee (or an affiliated licensee) has a financial interest, or when the licensee first learns the consumer will purchase that service
choice_b: Only at closing, as part of the settlement statement
choice_c: Only if the consumer affirmatively asks about referral relationships
choice_d: Within 30 days after the transaction closes
explanation: Section 606.1(a)(13) fixes the timing of the disclosure at the earlier of two triggers: when the licensee first recommends the consumer purchase the interested service, or when the licensee first learns the consumer will be purchasing it.

question: Under RELRA Section 606.1(a)(14), what must a licensee report to the Commission within 30 days of forming or joining a 'qualified association'?
choice_a: The association's name, its owners' names, the jurisdiction where it is registered, the date it was registered, and any changes in ownership
choice_b: No reporting obligation exists regarding qualified associations under RELRA
choice_c: The association's formation only if it generates more than $10,000 in annual revenue
choice_d: The association's formation to the local municipality, not the Commission, within 90 days
explanation: Section 606.1(a)(14) requires a licensee to report to the Commission, within 30 days of forming or joining a qualified association, that association's name, its owners' names, its jurisdiction of registration, the registration date, and any subsequent changes in ownership.

question: Under RELRA Section 606.1(b)(1), what must happen before a licensee is entitled to recover a fee, commission, or other valuable consideration paid by or on behalf of a consumer?
choice_a: The nature of the service and the fee to be charged must be set forth in a written agreement between the broker and the consumer, signed by the consumer -- though the licensee may still perform services before that agreement is signed, without being entitled to recover a fee absent the signed agreement
choice_b: A licensee may collect a fee based on a verbal agreement alone, provided a witness confirms the conversation
choice_c: A licensee may never perform any service before a written fee agreement is signed
choice_d: The written-agreement requirement applies only to listing agreements, never to buyer-representation agreements
explanation: Section 606.1(b)(1) bars a licensee from performing a compensated service for a consumer unless the service and fee are set out in a written agreement signed by the consumer, while allowing pre-agreement services -- just without a right to recover compensation absent that signed writing.

question: Under RELRA Section 606.1(b)(2), may a listing or buyer-agency agreement ever be oral rather than written?
choice_a: Yes -- an open listing agreement, or a nonexclusive buyer/tenant agency agreement, may be oral if the seller or buyer is provided a written memorandum stating the terms of the agreement
choice_b: No -- every listing and buyer-agency agreement in Pennsylvania must be in writing with no exceptions
choice_c: Yes, but only for commercial property transactions
choice_d: Yes, and no written memorandum of any kind is ever required
explanation: Section 606.1(b)(2) creates a narrow exception to the general written-agreement rule: an open listing or a nonexclusive buyer/tenant agency arrangement may be oral, provided the consumer is given a written memorandum stating the agreement's terms.

question: Under RELRA Section 606.1(b)(3), must a transaction licensee or subagent cooperating with the listing broker obtain a written agreement from the seller?
choice_a: No -- Section 606.1(b)(3) provides that nothing in the subsection requires a transaction licensee or subagent cooperating with the listing broker to obtain a written agreement from the seller
choice_b: Yes -- every subagent must independently obtain a signed written agreement from the seller before showing the property
choice_c: Only if the subagent intends to collect any portion of the commission
choice_d: Only in transactions involving vacant land
explanation: Section 606.1(b)(3) exempts a cooperating transaction licensee or subagent from needing its own written agreement with the seller -- the listing broker's agreement with the seller already covers that side of the transaction.

question: Under RELRA Section 606.1(b)(4), what must a subagent or transaction licensee who is cooperating with the listing broker for a fee paid by the listing broker or seller provide to the buyer before performing any services?
choice_a: A written disclosure statement, signed by the buyer, describing the nature of the services to be performed and containing the information required by Section 608 -- and if the buyer refuses to sign, the licensee must note the refusal on the statement and retain it for six months
choice_b: Nothing -- subagents cooperating with the listing broker owe no disclosure duty to the buyer
choice_c: A verbal explanation only, with no signature or retention requirement
choice_d: A written disclosure retained permanently, with no procedure specified for a buyer's refusal to sign
explanation: Section 606.1(b)(4) requires a fee-paid subagent or transaction licensee to give the buyer a signed written disclosure, containing the Section 608 information, before performing services -- and to document any refusal to sign and retain that record for six months.

question: Under RELRA Section 606.1(c), may a broker extend or delegate its agency relationship with a principal to another broker without the principal's consent?
choice_a: No -- a broker may not extend or delegate the broker's agency relationship with a principal to another broker without the principal's written consent
choice_b: Yes -- a broker may freely delegate its agency relationship to any cooperating broker without consent
choice_c: Yes, but only oral consent from the principal is required
choice_d: Only the Real Estate Commission, not the principal, must consent to such a delegation
explanation: Section 606.1(c) bars a broker from extending or delegating its agency relationship with a principal to another broker absent the principal's written consent -- protecting the principal's chosen agency relationship from being reassigned without their say-so.

question: Under RELRA Section 606.1(d), may a broker compensate another broker who assists in marketing and selling or leasing a consumer's property, and does that payment alone create an agency relationship?
choice_a: Yes, a broker may compensate another broker who assists in marketing/selling or leasing a consumer's property, but payment of compensation alone does not create an agency relationship between the consumer and that other broker
choice_b: No, compensating another broker is prohibited entirely under RELRA
choice_c: Yes, and doing so automatically creates a dual-agency relationship with the paid broker
choice_d: Only the listing broker may ever be compensated; cooperating brokers must work without pay
explanation: Section 606.1(d) permits compensation between cooperating brokers while making clear that payment alone does not, by itself, create an agency relationship between the consumer and the compensated broker.

question: Under RELRA Section 606.1(e), does a seller's-agent licensee who also presents alternative properties to prospective buyer/tenants breach any duty to the seller/landlord?
choice_a: No -- Section 606.1(e) states that presenting alternative properties does not in itself constitute a breach of any duty owed to the seller/landlord
choice_b: Yes -- showing any other property is an automatic breach of the exclusive listing
choice_c: Only if the seller pre-approves each alternative property shown
choice_d: This rule applies only to designated agents, not to standard seller's agents
explanation: Section 606.1(e) clarifies that a seller's-agent licensee who also shows alternative properties to prospective buyers is not, by that fact alone, breaching any duty owed to the seller/landlord -- the same principle Section 606.4(c) applies specifically to dual agents.

question: Under RELRA Section 606.1(f), does a buyer's-agent licensee who also presents alternative properties of interest to OTHER prospective buyer/tenants breach any duty to the original buyer/tenant?
choice_a: No -- Section 606.1(f) states that presenting the same alternative properties to other prospective buyer/tenants does not in itself breach any duty owed to that buyer/tenant
choice_b: Yes -- showing the same property to a competing buyer is always a breach of loyalty
choice_c: Only permitted with the original buyer's advance written waiver
choice_d: This provision applies solely to dual agents
explanation: Section 606.1(f) is the buyer's-agent mirror of Section 606.1(e): showing properties of interest to other prospective buyers does not, by itself, breach the duty owed to the original buyer/tenant.

question: Does RELRA Section 606.1(j) relieve a licensee of duties imposed by other provisions of the act?
choice_a: No -- Section 606.1(j) clarifies that nothing in that section relieves a licensee of any duty imposed by another provision of RELRA
choice_b: Yes -- Section 606.1 supersedes and replaces every other duty imposed elsewhere in RELRA
choice_c: The section is silent on how it interacts with other RELRA provisions
choice_d: Only duties imposed by Commission regulation, not other RELRA sections, survive Section 606.1
explanation: Section 606.1(j) is a savings clause: the general duties listed in that section are a floor, not a ceiling, and do not displace duties imposed by any other RELRA provision.

question: Under RELRA Section 606.2(2), is a seller's broker obligated to keep seeking additional offers once the property is already subject to an existing agreement for sale?
choice_a: No -- Section 606.2(2) provides a seller's broker is not obligated to seek additional offers to purchase the property while it is already subject to an existing agreement for sale
choice_b: Yes -- a seller's broker must always keep marketing and soliciting new offers, even after an agreement of sale is signed
choice_c: Only if the existing agreement of sale is contingent on financing
choice_d: The obligation to seek additional offers ends only at closing, not upon signing an agreement of sale
explanation: Section 606.2(2) requires a continuous, good-faith marketing effort from a seller's agent, but expressly relieves the broker of seeking additional offers once the property is already under an existing agreement for sale.

question: Under RELRA Section 606.3(1)-(2), what loyalty and search duties does a buyer's broker owe, and what is the exception to the search duty?
choice_a: To be loyal to the buyer by taking action consistent with the buyer's interest, and to make a continuous, good-faith effort to find a property for the buyer -- except that the buyer's broker need not seek additional properties while the buyer is already subject to an existing contract to purchase
choice_b: To remain neutral between the buyer and any competing buyers represented by the same firm
choice_c: To seek additional properties for the buyer at all times, even after a contract for sale is signed
choice_d: No loyalty duty applies to a buyer's broker beyond the general duties in Section 606.1
explanation: Section 606.3(1)-(2) mirrors the seller's-agent loyalty and search duties of Section 606.2, applied to buyer's brokers: loyalty to the buyer and a continuous good-faith search for a property, except once the buyer already has an existing contract to purchase.

question: Under RELRA Section 606.4(b)(1), what is a dual agent prohibited from doing?
choice_a: Taking any action that is adverse or detrimental to either party's interest in the transaction
choice_b: Taking whatever action most benefits the party who is paying the commission
choice_c: Taking any action of any kind on behalf of either party -- a dual agent must remain entirely passive
choice_d: Favoring the buyer's interest over the seller's interest whenever the two conflict
explanation: Section 606.4(b)(1) requires a dual agent to take no action adverse or detrimental to either party's interest -- the core neutrality principle underlying Pennsylvania's disclosed-dual-agency framework.

question: Under RELRA Section 606.4(b)(2)-(3), what marketing/search duties does a dual agent owe to each side, and how can those duties be modified?
choice_a: Unless otherwise agreed to in writing, to make a continuous good-faith effort to find a buyer for the property AND a continuous good-faith effort to find a property for the buyer -- subject to the same existing-contract exceptions that apply to single-agency relationships
choice_b: A dual agent has no marketing or search duty of any kind toward either party
choice_c: A dual agent must obtain new written consent from both parties every 30 days to continue any marketing effort
choice_d: The continuous-good-faith-effort duty may only be waived by the seller, never by the buyer
explanation: Section 606.4(b)(2)-(3) requires a dual agent to make continuous good-faith efforts on BOTH sides (finding a buyer and finding a property), unless otherwise agreed to in writing, subject to the same existing-contract carve-outs found in the single-agency provisions.

question: Under RELRA Section 606.5(b)(1), what loyalty duty does a designated agent owe?
choice_a: To be loyal to the principal with whom the agent is working, by taking action consistent with that principal's interest in the transaction
choice_b: To remain equally loyal to both principals in the transaction, since both are clients of the same broker
choice_c: To defer all negotiating decisions to the broker rather than to the assigned principal
choice_d: No loyalty duty applies until the transaction reaches the agreement-of-sale stage
explanation: Section 606.5(b)(1) requires a designated agent to be loyal specifically to the principal they were designated to represent, taking action consistent with that principal's interest -- unlike the broker itself, who is treated as a dual agent.

question: Under RELRA Section 606.5(b)(2), what search/marketing duty does a designated agent owe, and what are its exceptions?
choice_a: To make a continuous, good-faith effort to find a buyer for a seller principal or a property for a buyer principal -- except that the designated agent need not seek additional offers for a seller principal under an existing contract for sale, or additional properties for a buyer principal already under an existing contract to purchase
choice_b: To seek additional offers or properties at all times, without exception, even after a contract exists
choice_c: No search/marketing duty applies to designated agents, only to non-designated agents
choice_d: The duty applies only to designated agents representing sellers, not to those representing buyers
explanation: Section 606.5(b)(2) requires the same continuous good-faith search duty (and the same existing-contract exceptions) that apply to single-agency seller's and buyer's agents under Sections 606.2 and 606.3.

question: Under RELRA Section 606.6(1), what must a transaction licensee advise the consumer being assisted?
choice_a: That the licensee is not acting as an agent or advocate of the consumer and should not be provided with confidential information
choice_b: That the licensee is acting as a full fiduciary agent, identical to a buyer's or seller's agent
choice_c: No advisory duty applies to transaction licensees under Section 606.6
choice_d: That the licensee will advise the consumer only after the transaction has closed
explanation: Section 606.6(1) requires a transaction licensee to affirmatively advise the consumer that the licensee is not their agent or advocate and should not be given confidential information -- laying the groundwork for the 'limited confidentiality' duty in Section 606.6(2).

question: Under RELRA Section 608(a)(3), what right regarding the scope of a broker's services must the initial-interview disclosure describe?
choice_a: That a real estate consumer has the right to enter into a negotiated agreement with the broker limiting the activities or practices the broker will provide, with fee and services determined by negotiation between consumer and broker
choice_b: That all broker services are fixed by Commission regulation and cannot be limited by agreement
choice_c: That only sellers, not buyers, may negotiate limited-service agreements
choice_d: No such right exists; Section 608 addresses only fee disclosure, not service scope
explanation: Section 608(a)(3) requires the initial-interview disclosure to inform the consumer of their right to negotiate a limited-service agreement with the broker, with both fee and scope of services subject to negotiation.

question: Under RELRA Section 608(a)(4), what must the initial-interview disclosure state about the possibility that the broker may serve another consumer in the same transaction?
choice_a: A statement identifying that possibility, explaining the duties the broker may owe the other party and whether the broker may accept a fee for those services
choice_b: A statement guaranteeing the broker will never represent more than one party to any transaction
choice_c: A statement listing every other current client the broker represents, regardless of transaction
choice_d: This disclosure is required only in commercial transactions
explanation: Section 608(a)(4) requires the initial-interview disclosure to flag the possibility that the broker may serve another consumer in the same transaction and explain the resulting duties and any fee the broker may accept -- distinct from Section 608(a)(5)'s designated-agency-specific flag.

question: Under RELRA Section 608(a)(6), what must the initial-interview disclosure state about the broker's relationship with other brokers?
choice_a: A statement of the broker's policies regarding cooperation with other brokers, including the sharing of fees
choice_b: A statement of the broker's personal income for the prior calendar year
choice_c: A statement barring cooperation with any other brokerage
choice_d: This disclosure is required only for buyer's brokers, not for listing brokers
explanation: Section 608(a)(6) requires the initial-interview disclosure to describe the broker's cooperation policies with other brokers, including fee-sharing practices -- giving the consumer visibility into how the broker works with the rest of the market.

question: Under RELRA Section 608(a)(7), what must the initial-interview disclosure state about a buyer's broker's compensation and role?
choice_a: That a buyer's broker may be paid a fee that is a percentage of the purchase price, and that the buyer's broker, even if compensated by the listing broker, will represent the interests of the buyer
choice_b: That a buyer's broker may never be compensated as a percentage of the purchase price
choice_c: That being paid by the listing broker automatically converts the buyer's broker into a subagent of the seller
choice_d: That buyer's brokers are barred from receiving any compensation from the listing broker
explanation: Section 608(a)(7) requires disclosure that a buyer's broker may earn a percentage-of-price fee and still represents the buyer's interests even when compensated by the listing broker -- reassuring consumers that compensation source does not flip loyalty.

question: Under RELRA Section 608(a)(9), what must the initial-interview disclosure include regarding the Real Estate Recovery Fund?
choice_a: The purpose of the Real Estate Recovery Fund and the telephone number of the Commission where further information about the fund may be obtained
choice_b: The current account balance of the Real Estate Recovery Fund
choice_c: A list of every claim ever paid from the Real Estate Recovery Fund
choice_d: This disclosure is not required at the initial interview -- it applies only to the written agreement under Section 608.1
explanation: Section 608(a)(9) requires the initial-interview disclosure to explain the Real Estate Recovery Fund's purpose and provide the Commission's phone number for more information -- a disclosure repeated again in the written-agreement requirements of Section 608.1(6).

question: Under RELRA Section 608(a)(11), when must a sales agreement contain the zoning classification of the property?
choice_a: Always, except when the property (or each subdividable parcel) is zoned solely or primarily to permit single-family dwellings
choice_b: Only for commercial properties
choice_c: The disclosure is optional and left to the broker's discretion
choice_d: Never, if the buyer is represented by counsel
explanation: Section 608(a)(11) requires the initial-interview disclosure to flag that a sales agreement must contain the property's zoning classification, unless the property is zoned solely/primarily for single-family dwellings -- a requirement enforced with real teeth in the related sales-contract provision, Section 608.2(3).

question: Under RELRA Section 608(c), what must a licensee do if the initial interview with a consumer does not occur in person?
choice_a: Orally advise the consumer of the various business relationships the licensee may have with the consumer, using the statute's prescribed oral disclosure explaining that information shared before the written consumer notice is provided is not considered confidential unless and until a business relationship is formed
choice_b: No disclosure of any kind is required if the initial interview occurs over the phone
choice_c: Mail the written disclosure form before any conversation may occur
choice_d: The oral-disclosure requirement applies only to commercial transactions
explanation: Section 608(c) supplies specific scripted language a licensee must use when the initial interview happens by phone or otherwise not in person, warning the consumer that pre-relationship information is not confidential.

question: Under RELRA Section 608(d), if a licensee gives the oral disclosure described in Section 608(c), by when must the written disclosure form still be provided to the consumer?
choice_a: No later than the earlier of the first in-person meeting the licensee has with the consumer after the initial interview, or the time a property is first shown to the consumer by the licensee or anyone working with the licensee
choice_b: Within 30 days of the initial interview, regardless of any in-person meeting or showing
choice_c: No written form is ever required once an oral disclosure under Section 608(c) has been given
choice_d: The written disclosure must be provided before the oral disclosure, not after
explanation: Section 608(d) sets an outer time limit on the written disclosure that must follow an oral one: whichever comes first between the next in-person meeting or the first property showing.

question: Under RELRA Section 608(e), what disclosure applies instead of the standard Section 608(a) form when a licensee is showing a time-share estate?
choice_a: A written 'CONSUMER NOTICE -- THIS IS NOT A CONTRACT' statement indicating the capacity in which the licensee is acting, provided at the time of the initial interview
choice_b: Time-share transactions are entirely exempt from any disclosure under RELRA
choice_c: A full written buyer-agency agreement instead of any notice
choice_d: The time-share carve-out applies only if the buyer is a Pennsylvania resident
explanation: Section 608(e) creates a time-share-specific alternative to the standard Section 608(a) disclosure, closely modeled on the rental Consumer Notice in Section 608(b): a written notice, headed 'THIS IS NOT A CONTRACT,' identifying the licensee's capacity.

question: Under RELRA Section 608(f), do the initial-interview disclosures required by subsections (a), (b), and (c) apply in a commercial property sale or lease transaction?
choice_a: No, unless the prospective buyer/tenant or seller/landlord is an individual
choice_b: Yes, always, with no exception for commercial transactions
choice_c: The commercial exception applies only to lease transactions, never to sales
choice_d: The commercial exception applies only if the transaction value exceeds $1 million
explanation: Section 608(f) exempts commercial property sale or lease transactions from the Section 608(a), (b), and (c) disclosure requirements, unless the buyer/tenant or seller/landlord involved happens to be an individual rather than a business entity.

question: Under RELRA Section 608.1, what two things must a written agreement between a broker and a fee-paying consumer contain, at a minimum?
choice_a: The consumer's signature, and identification of the services to be provided and the fee to be paid, if any
choice_b: Only a verbal acknowledgment of the fee, not a signed writing
choice_c: The written agreement need only identify the services provided, never the fee
choice_d: Section 608.1 applies only to seller listing agreements, never to buyer-agency agreements
explanation: Section 608.1 requires any Section 606.1(b)-triggered written agreement to be signed by the consumer and to identify both the services to be provided and the fee to be paid, before layering on the seven additional required disclosures in paragraphs (1)-(7).

question: Under RELRA Section 608.1(1), what must the written agreement state about how the broker's fee and contract duration were determined?
choice_a: That the broker's fee and the duration of the contract have been determined as a result of negotiations between the broker and the seller/landlord or buyer/tenant
choice_b: That the broker's fee is set by state regulation and not subject to negotiation
choice_c: That the duration of the contract is fixed at one year by default
choice_d: No statement about negotiation is required in the written agreement itself
explanation: Section 608.1(1) requires the written agreement to affirmatively state that both the fee and the contract duration were reached through negotiation between broker and consumer.

question: Under RELRA Section 608.1(2), what must the written agreement describe about the broker's services?
choice_a: The nature and extent of the broker's services to be provided to the seller/landlord or buyer/tenant, and the fees that will be charged
choice_b: Only the broker's office address and phone number
choice_c: The broker's marketing budget for the specific listing
choice_d: This disclosure is optional and left to the broker's discretion
explanation: Section 608.1(2) requires the written agreement to describe the nature and extent of the services the broker will provide, along with the fees to be charged for them.

question: Under RELRA Section 608.1(3), what must the written agreement disclose about the possibility of the broker serving more than one consumer in a single transaction?
choice_a: A statement identifying any such possibility, explaining the duties that may be owed the other party and whether the broker may accept a fee for those services
choice_b: A guarantee that the broker will never represent more than one consumer in the same transaction
choice_c: A statement disclosing the identity of every other client the broker currently represents
choice_d: This disclosure applies only to commercial transactions
explanation: Section 608.1(3) requires the same kind of multiple-representation disclosure required at the initial interview under Section 608(a)(4), now built into the written agreement itself.

question: Under RELRA Section 608.1(4), what must an agreement between a broker and a SELLER disclose regarding cooperating buyer agents and dual agency?
choice_a: The broker's policies on cooperating with subagents and buyer agents, a disclosure that a buyer agent -- even if compensated by the broker or seller -- will represent the buyer's interests, and a disclosure of any potential for the broker to act as a disclosed dual agent
choice_b: A statement that the broker will never cooperate with buyer agents under any circumstances
choice_c: A guarantee that the broker will not act as a dual agent under any circumstances
choice_d: This disclosure is required only in buyer agreements, not in seller agreements
explanation: Section 608.1(4) requires seller agreements to disclose the broker's cooperation policy, confirm that a buyer agent still represents the buyer regardless of who pays them, and flag any potential dual-agency scenario.

question: Under RELRA Section 608.1(5), what must an agreement between a broker and a BUYER disclose regarding compensation and dual agency?
choice_a: A statement identifying any possibility the broker's compensation may be based on a percentage of the purchase price, a disclosure of the broker's cooperation policies with listing brokers willing to pay buyer's brokers, a disclosure that the broker -- even if paid by the listing broker or seller -- will represent the buyer's interests, and a disclosure of any potential for the buyer broker to act as a disclosed dual agent
choice_b: A statement that the broker's compensation may never be tied to the purchase price
choice_c: A guarantee that the broker will never accept compensation from the listing broker
choice_d: This disclosure is required only in seller agreements, not in buyer agreements
explanation: Section 608.1(5) is the buyer-side mirror of Section 608.1(4): it requires disclosure of percentage-of-price compensation possibilities, cooperation policy with listing brokers, continued representation of the buyer regardless of payment source, and potential dual agency.

question: Under RELRA Section 608.1(6), must a written broker agreement describe the Real Estate Recovery Fund, given that it was already covered at the initial interview under Section 608(a)(9)?
choice_a: Yes -- Section 608.1(6) separately requires a statement describing the purpose of the Real Estate Recovery Fund established under Section 801 and the Commission's telephone number for further information
choice_b: No -- the written agreement need not mention the Real Estate Recovery Fund at all, since it was already disclosed at the initial interview
choice_c: Only a statement of the fund's current account balance and number of pending claims is required
choice_d: A statement waiving the consumer's right to file a claim against the fund is required
explanation: Section 608.1(6) requires the Recovery Fund disclosure again in the written agreement itself, independent of the initial-interview disclosure required under Section 608(a)(9) -- the two requirements are cumulative, not either/or.

question: Under RELRA Section 608.1(7), what must the written agreement state about conflicts of interest?
choice_a: A statement regarding any possible conflicts of interest and informing the consumer of the licensee's continuing duty to timely disclose any conflicts of interest
choice_b: That conflicts of interest need be disclosed only once, at signing, with no continuing duty thereafter
choice_c: That conflicts of interest are addressed exclusively through Commission investigation, not broker disclosure
choice_d: This disclosure is optional and may be omitted with the consumer's oral consent
explanation: Section 608.1(7) requires the written agreement to address conflicts of interest and confirm the licensee's ongoing (not one-time) duty to timely disclose them -- reinforcing the general duty already imposed by Section 606.1(a)(7).

question: Under RELRA Section 608.3(a), what must a comparative market analysis (CMA) contain, and where must it appear?
choice_a: Printed conspicuously and without change on the first page, a statement that the analysis was not performed under the Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal Practice, is not to be construed as an appraisal, and may not be used as such for any purpose
choice_b: No disclaimer is required, since a CMA is understood to be an informal document
choice_c: The required disclaimer may be placed anywhere in the document, including the final page, at the preparer's discretion
choice_d: A certification that the analysis WAS performed under the Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal Practice
explanation: Section 608.3(a) mandates specific, conspicuous first-page disclaimer language on every CMA, distinguishing it clearly from a certified appraisal governed by USPAP.

question: Under RELRA Section 608.3(b), is a comparative market analysis prepared in accordance with RELRA deemed to be an appraisal within the scope of the Real Estate Appraisers Certification Act?
choice_a: No -- Section 608.3(b) provides that a CMA prepared in accordance with RELRA is not deemed to be an appraisal within the scope of the Real Estate Appraisers Certification Act
choice_b: Yes -- any CMA prepared by a licensee is automatically treated as a certified appraisal
choice_c: Only CMAs prepared by brokers who also hold a separate appraiser certification are exempt from appraisal-act treatment
choice_d: The statute does not address the relationship between CMAs and the Real Estate Appraisers Certification Act
explanation: Section 608.3(b) shields a properly prepared CMA from being reclassified as an appraisal under the separate Real Estate Appraisers Certification Act, so long as it follows RELRA's requirements (including the Section 608.3(a) disclaimer).

question: Under RELRA Section 608.3(c), to whom must any fee charged for a comparative market analysis be paid?
choice_a: The broker
choice_b: Directly to the individual salesperson who prepared it, bypassing the broker
choice_c: RELRA prohibits charging any fee for a comparative market analysis
choice_d: Into the Real Estate Recovery Fund
explanation: Section 608.3(c) requires that any CMA fee be paid to the broker -- consistent with RELRA's general framework of the broker, not the individual salesperson, as the party entitled to compensation.

question: Under RELRA Section 608(b)(1), which three categories of licensees may use the rental-only 'Consumer Notice' disclosure instead of the standard Section 608(a) form?
choice_a: The actual owner/landlord of the property (including an equity-interest owner in the owner/landlord), a direct employee of the owner/landlord, or a licensee leasing the property under a property management or exclusive leasing agreement with the owner/landlord
choice_b: Only a fully licensed broker acting for a fee may use the rental Consumer Notice
choice_c: Any licensee showing any rental property, regardless of their relationship to the owner
choice_d: Only licensees who are also members of the Real Estate Commission
explanation: Section 608(b)(1) limits the rental-only Consumer Notice carve-out to three specific categories of licensee-owner relationships: actual owner/equity-interest holder, direct employee of the owner, or an agent under a property-management/exclusive-leasing agreement.

question: Under RELRA Section 608(b)(3), what retention and refusal procedure applies to the rental-only Consumer Notice?
choice_a: The licensee must provide a copy of the signed statement to the prospective tenant and retain a copy signed by both the tenant and the licensee for six months; if the tenant refuses to sign, the licensee must note the refusal on the form and retain it for six months
choice_b: No retention obligation applies to the rental Consumer Notice once it is delivered
choice_c: The signed notice must be retained permanently, with no six-month minimum
choice_d: If the tenant refuses to sign, the licensee may not proceed with the rental transaction at all
explanation: Section 608(b)(3) sets a uniform six-month retention rule for the rental Consumer Notice, whether signed by the tenant or noted as a refusal -- mirroring the identical six-month retention procedure for the buyer disclosure under Section 606.1(b)(4).
